claim: When a jailbreak attack succeeds against a safety-aligned LLM, the model's safety-relevant internal representations are not eliminated — they are bypassed. The attack selectively suppresses a small subset of attention heads, and suppressing that subset is by itself enough to turn a refusal into a compliance, while other heads go on representing the harmful content even as the attack succeeds. Because those representations persist, they can be read out directly as a harmful-input detector, with no additional training, at a quality competitive with dedicated safety models.
experiments_evaluated: To address subclaims 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 8, and 9, run a paired activation/readout study on an open safety-aligned model such as Llama-2-7B-Chat, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, or Mistral-Instruct. Use public harmful-intent datasets such as HarmBench or AdvBench, benign controls from Alpaca/ShareGPT, and public jailbreak templates or labeled attacks from JailbreakBench/JailbreakHub. For each harmful request, create paired inputs: the plain harmful request, a jailbreak-wrapped version that actually elicits non-refusal, and benign controls with similar surface form. Record residual-stream states and per-head outputs at each layer during the prompt and early generation. Then test whether harmfulness remains linearly or directly readable in successful jailbreak cases using only pre-specified, non-trained readouts: e.g., logit-lens scores for fixed unsafe-category label tokens, cosine similarity to unembedding-derived harmfulness/refusal directions, or nearest-neighbor retrieval against frozen model activations without fitting parameters. Evaluate whether these readouts distinguish successful jailbroken harmful inputs from benign inputs, and compare AUROC/F1 to public dedicated safety classifiers such as Llama Guard, ShieldGemma, or HarmBench classifiers. If harmfulness is still detectable in successful jailbreak activations at competitive quality, this supports persistence and direct readout; if detection collapses to benign levels, this supports elimination or strong obfuscation; if only trained probes work, it weakens the no additional training subclaim. This experiment could be made unnecessary by publicly released activation traces and train-free detector benchmarks showing the same comparison on matched successful jailbreaks and benign controls.

To address subclaims 4 and 5, perform causal head-localization and intervention experiments on the same successful jailbreak/plain-refusal prompt pairs. First identify candidate attention heads whose outputs, attention patterns, or activation norms are selectively reduced during successful jailbreak prompts relative to plain harmful prompts that refuse, while controlling for prompt length and position. Rank heads using activation patching, attribution patching, or path patching with refusal/compliance logit-difference as the metric. Then test causality: suppress only the top-k candidate heads on plain harmful prompts by zero-ablation or mean-ablation and measure whether the model changes from refusal toward compliance; conversely, restore or patch those heads from the plain-refusal run into the jailbroken run and measure whether refusal returns. Vary k to test the small subset claim. If a small, stable set of heads is both selectively suppressed by jailbreaks and causally sufficient to flip refusal/compliance, the subclaims are supported; if many heads are required, the effect is diffuse; if suppression is correlational and patching does not change behavior, the claim is weakened. This experiment could be made unnecessary by a reproducible circuit-discovery artifact giving head indices, patching code, and intervention effect sizes across public models and datasets.

With respect to evidence pieces 8 and 9, test whether the proposed bypass mechanism generalizes beyond one attack family by repeating the activation and head-intervention analyses across different jailbreak types, including multi-turn attention-shifting attacks and continuation-triggered jailbreaks, using public datasets or prompts from JailbreakBench, HarmBench, and the papers' released artifacts if available. For each attack class, measure three quantities on matched successful and failed attacks: persistence of harmful-content readouts in non-suppressed heads, suppression magnitude of the candidate refusal-mediating heads, and causal flip rates under head ablation/restoration. Also test cross-attack transfer: heads discovered on one jailbreak type should predict or causally affect behavior on another if the claim describes a general mechanism. If the same small head subset and persistent harmful representations appear across attack families and models, the broad bypass account is strengthened; if each attack uses different components, the claim may hold only locally; if continuation or multi-turn attacks show representation loss rather than bypass, the general claim fails. This experiment could be made unnecessary by stronger existing evidence from papers 8 and 9 reporting cross-attack, cross-model causal interventions rather than only behavioral jailbreak success rates.
reference_experiments: Before identifying any component, test the premise that attacks bypass rather than erase safety representations. On inputs where a jailbreak succeeded, measure activation of the refusal direction across all layers and components (attention heads and MLPs) and compare against the same requests unattacked. If a successful attack flattens refusal activation everywhere, attacks do break safety representations and everything downstream is dead. The authors find mid layers still maintain substantial refusal activation under successful attack, particularly in the layers previously identified as most safety-relevant.

Construct the paired evaluation set the whole analysis depends on. Sample benign prompts from Alpaca, collect harmful behaviours from published harmful-behaviour datasets, generate attack variants with GCG, AutoDAN, many-shot jailbreaking and PAIR, and retain only pairs where the unattacked request is refused and the attacked version succeeds. Within-pair comparison is what separates the attack's effect from differences between requests. The authors obtain 378 (Llama-2-7B-Chat) and 176 (Llama-3-8B-Instruct) usable pairs from roughly 10,000 attack samples, a 2-3% yield that caps the study's statistical power.

Build and calibrate the component-scoring instrument. Extract the refusal direction by difference-in-means and select the optimal layer, project it into each attention head's output space to score that head's contribution to the refusal signal, and classify heads by distribution overlap between conditions using two-stage filtering. Then verify the classification is not an artifact of the cut point by sweeping the threshold and the KDE bandwidth. The authors use thresholds of 0.5, find stability across 0.4-0.6, and obtain 21 ACHs and 17 SAHs for Llama-3 (416 heads analysed) and 20 ACHs and 19 SAHs for Llama-2 (480 analysed), with ACHs concentrated in layers 0-3 and SAHs in layers 5-12.

Test causally whether suppressing the identified heads is sufficient to cause attack success. On harmful inputs the model normally refuses (baseline ASR about 0%), inject a negative refusal-direction feature into ACH outputs, progressively increase the number of intervened heads, and measure attack success rate — with a matched random-head intervention as control, 10 seeds and 95% confidence intervals. Without the random-head arm the effect cannot be attributed to those heads rather than to perturbing that many heads at all. The authors report ACH intervention driving ASR to 99.5% (Llama-3) and 83.7% (Llama-2), reaching 95.0% and 81.6% at just 8 heads, against 4.0% +/- 3.7 and 10.2% +/- 11.6 for random heads.

Test whether the other head type is a real source of the persistent signal. Apply the same suppression to SAHs, this time on attack inputs, and measure the change in mid-layer activation strength using mean absolute activation across mid-layer heads. The authors report Llama-2 falling from 0.222 to 0.181 (18%) and Llama-3 from 0.0062 to 0.0053 (14%), against a reference of 0.397 and 0.0086 under unattacked harmful inputs.

Discriminate the mechanistic account from the rival explanation that the two head types simply differ in sensitivity to harmful content. Using the linearity of attention, attribute each head's activation to individual input tokens, separate the contribution of the original harmful-request tokens from that of the attack-template tokens, and compare the two head types on each. The account holds only if the types are indistinguishable on the harmful request itself and separate sharply on the attack template. The authors report medians within +/-0.15 on harmful tokens, against roughly -1.5 for ACHs and +1.5 for SAHs on attack-template tokens.

Validate externally that the persistent signal generalises and is useful. Build a training-free detector that reads standardised activations at discriminative positions via top-m aggregation and thresholds the score, then evaluate Macro-F1 on ten safety-eval benchmarks across six models from three architecture families, against both the model's own refusal behaviour and trained guard models. If the readout does not transfer, the phenomenon is a property of the two models analysed. The authors report Gemma-2B improving from 0.470 to 0.853 and Qwen-7B from 0.506 to 0.860 overall, SALAD-Bench from 0.270 to 0.976, and Llama-3-8B reaching 0.888 weighted average against WildGuard 0.880 and LlamaGuard3/4 at 0.599/0.666.

reference_coverage.rationale: The paired activation study records residual-stream and per-head states throughout the network for plain refused and successful jailbroken versions, and offers fixed refusal/harmfulness readouts. The cross-attack study additionally measures persistent readouts in non-suppressed heads. This provides the same persistence-versus-erasure discrimination without requiring the reference's particular direction statistic.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A component-level localization procedure that ranks attention heads by attack-induced changes relative to refusal, identifies a small differentiated subset, and checks that the localization is not merely an arbitrary choice of components.

These are alternative component-scoring and stability routes with comparable discriminating power; the reference's particular overlap statistic and threshold sweep are implementation choices rather than claim requirements.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A causal intervention on the localized small subset, with a dose-response over subset size and a control showing that the behavioral flip is specific to those heads rather than generic perturbation.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposals do test top-k suppression on normally refused harmful prompts, measure refusal-to-compliance flips, vary k, and add restoration and cross-attack checks. They do not include a matched random-head or other nonspecific-intervention control, nor comparable repeated uncertainty estimates. Thus the intervention can show that perturbing the selected heads can flip behavior, but cannot cleanly establish that the selected subset is responsible rather than that any perturbation of that size is effective.
reasoning_chain: [1] The reference experiment establishes causal sufficiency of the selected subset relative to generic perturbation by including a matched control intervention.
[2] Proposed experiments 1 and 2 ablate or patch selected heads and measure behavioral flips, so they do bear directly on causal sufficiency.
[3] Neither proposed experiment specifies a random-head or matched nonspecific control, and neither supplies the reference-level repeated uncertainty protocol.
[4] A large flip rate could therefore be caused by the strength or number of perturbed heads rather than the selected subset itself.
[5] The team would fail to learn whether the selected heads specifically, rather than generic head perturbation, are sufficient to turn refusal into compliance.

evidence.bearing: Shows the reference’s explicit decision rule and sensitivity test that the proposed ranking description omits.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A causal dose-response intervention on the candidate heads, compared with an equally sized nonspecific intervention and repeated uncertainty estimates, showing that suppressing the selected small subset—not merely perturbing that many heads—is sufficient to cause compliance.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 1 ablates top-k heads on normally refusing harmful prompts, measures the refusal-to-compliance flip, and adds a restoration intervention; experiment 2 repeats causal tests across attack classes and models. But there is no matched random-head or other nonspecific-head control and no stated repeated-seed confidence analysis. A compliance increase could therefore result from generic disruption caused by intervening in any heads, leaving the selective causal attribution ambiguous.
reasoning_chain: [1] The reference causal result attributes the behavior change to the selected subset by comparing it with random heads under repeated trials.
[2] The proposed ablation compares selected-head intervention with no intervention and optionally restoration, but does not perturb matched random heads.
[3] Without that control, a high flip rate is compatible with a generic effect of zeroing or mean-ablating several heads rather than a property of the selected subset.
[4] The team would learn that the proposed intervention can change behavior, but would fail to learn that the subset itself is selectively sufficient.

evidence.quote: For ACHs, we simulate attack effects on harmful inputs (baseline ASR ≈ 0%) by injecting a negative feature ... We use random heads as control (10 seeds, 95% CIs).
evidence.bearing: Establishes the matched nonspecific control and uncertainty structure needed for the reference causal inference.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A causal suppression test on heads that remain active during successful attacks, measuring whether their removal reduces the residual mid-layer safety signal and thereby establishing them as its source rather than merely observing correlation.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed activation studies observe persistent readouts in non-suppressed heads and measure candidate-head suppression across attack conditions, so they bear on persistence. They do not, however, suppress the persistent/non-suppressed head group and measure the resulting mid-layer activation. Thus persistent activity could be correlated with, rather than generating, the signal; the team would fail to learn the causal source of that signal.
reasoning_chain: [1] The reference experiment identifies the contribution of the heads that remain active by suppressing them during successful attacks and measuring the loss of the mid-layer signal.
[2] Proposed experiments 0 and 2 measure readouts in non-suppressed heads but leave those heads intact.
[3] Observing a persistent readout without perturbing its purported source cannot distinguish source from a downstream correlate or residual signal generated elsewhere.
[4] The team would learn that some non-suppressed representations persist, but would fail to learn whether those heads causally supply the persistent signal.

evidence.quote: SAH Ablation: Validating the Source of Robust Activations Figure 6 shows that ablating SAHs substantially weakens mid-layer activations.
evidence.bearing: Establishes that the reference uses ablation specifically to test source, not just persistence.

reference_coverage.adequacy: An additive token-level attribution that separately measures the contribution of original harmful-request tokens and attack-template tokens for the two component types, ruling out the explanation that the types merely have different intrinsic harmful-content sensitivity.
reference_coverage.rationale: None of the proposed experiments decomposes head activations by token origin. Comparing whole prompts, attack classes, or prompt length/position can reveal attack-associated suppression, but cannot determine whether the difference comes from attack-template tokens versus the original harmful request. The proposed set would therefore fail to learn the reference experiment’s mechanistic discrimination.
reasoning_chain: [1] The reference experiment separates original harmful-request-token contributions from attack-template-token contributions to distinguish selective attack effects from ordinary content sensitivity.
[2] Proposed experiments compare complete plain and jailbreak prompts and aggregate head or readout behavior, without additive token attribution or token-origin grouping.
[3] Whole-prompt differences leave the rival explanation open because the added template and the harmful request are not separately measured.
[4] The team would fail to learn whether the component split is caused specifically by attack-template tokens rather than by different sensitivity to harmful content.

evidence.quote: On the original harmful tokens, ACHs and SAHs exhibit similar activation distributions ... However, attack-template tokens induce drastically different effects: ACHs are strongly suppressed ...
evidence.bearing: States the specific token-origin distinction made by the reference and absent from the proposed set.

reference_coverage.adequacy: An evaluation of a fixed, training-free internal-activation detector on harmful and benign data across attack and ordinary settings, using standard discrimination metrics and direct comparison with independently trained safety models, with enough model or attack diversity to assess usefulness beyond one case.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 0 specifies non-trained readouts, evaluates AUROC/F1 on public harmful and jailbreak data with benign controls, and compares them with dedicated safety classifiers. Experiment 2 adds cross-attack and cross-model transfer checks for the same readouts. This supplies the relevant detector utility and comparator evidence without requiring the exact benchmark suite, model list, or detector statistic used by the reference.

It would not, however, settle the full mechanistic claim as written: selected-head intervention lacks a nonspecific control, the persistent-head source is not causally tested, component selection lacks the reference’s calibration robustness, and the token-level rival explanation remains untested.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A reproducible and validated way to localize a small set of heads with distinct behavior under successful attacks, while checking that the localization is not an arbitrary ranking or unstable choice.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed causal-localization study ranks heads using activation or patching-based behaviorally relevant criteria, tests candidate heads directly, varies the number intervened, and requires stability across attack classes and models. This is a different but comparably discriminating route from threshold and bandwidth sweeps for identifying a localized head subset.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A causal sufficiency test showing that manipulating only the localized small subset flips a normally refused harmful request to compliance, with protection against interpreting generic perturbation as head-specific causation.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 1 performs the central top-k ablation and measures refusal-to-compliance flips, and its converse restoration/patching provides a useful bidirectional causal check. However, it does not include a matched same-size arbitrary-head or other nonspecific perturbation control, and experiment 2 repeats the candidate intervention without adding that control. A flip would therefore establish that the candidate manipulation can be sufficient, but leave its specificity relative to generic head disruption ambiguous.
reasoning_chain: The reference experiment establishes not merely that some intervention can cause compliance, but that the localized subset is responsible rather than an arbitrary perturbation of the same number of heads.
The proposed set ablates only the selected candidates and measures the behavioral flip, but supplies no matched random-head or equivalent nonspecific intervention.
Bidirectional restoration strengthens the causal case but does not quantify whether an arbitrary same-size perturbation would produce the same flip.

Therefore the team would learn that the selected intervention can turn refusal into compliance, but would fail to learn decisively whether the claimed subset is specifically responsible for that effect.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A causal test of whether the non-suppressed safety-relevant head population contributes to the persistent internal signal, by suppressing that population and measuring the resulting change in the signal.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed studies measure harmful-content readouts in non-suppressed heads and thus directly examine whether a persistent signal is present there. They do not suppress that other population and measure the signal change; the listed interventions target the candidate refusal-mediating heads. The proposal can show representation persists in other heads, but cannot establish the causal contribution that the reference intervention tested.
reasoning_chain: The reference experiment asks whether the other head population is a causal source of the persistent signal, not only whether a readout is observable in those heads.
Proposed experiments 0 and 2 observe readouts in non-suppressed heads, but their suppressions and restorations are directed at candidate refusal-mediating heads.
An observed non-suppressed-head readout is compatible with those heads being causal, redundant, or merely correlated with signal carried elsewhere.
Thus the team would learn about persistence in other heads, but would fail to learn whether suppressing that population itself reduces the persistent signal.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A token-resolved attribution that separates the original harmful-request contribution from the jailbreak-template contribution, allowing differential head responses to harmful content and attack steering to be distinguished.
reference_coverage.rationale: The paired prompts, position/length controls, cross-attack comparisons, and head interventions get at the mechanistic alternative indirectly. But no proposed experiment decomposes each head's activation into original-request tokens versus attack-template tokens, so a difference between full prompts could still reflect different sensitivity to the changed harmful-content context rather than the proposed bypass mechanism.
reasoning_chain: The reference experiment discriminates bypass from the rival explanation that the head types simply differ in sensitivity to harmful content by isolating token sources.
The proposed set compares whole plain and jailbreak-wrapped prompts and controls some surface properties, but never attributes activations separately to harmful-request and attack-template tokens.
Consequently, a successful localization and intervention result could still be explained by head sensitivity to the changed full input rather than selective processing of the attack template.
The team would therefore fail to resolve this mechanistic rival as cleanly as the reference experiment.

reference_coverage.adequacy: An externally evaluated, training-free harmful-input readout tested on successful jailbreaks and benign or harmful controls across sufficiently varied models and evaluation sets, with a direct comparison to dedicated safety detectors.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 0 prespecifies readouts with no fitted parameters, evaluates AUROC/F1 on successful jailbreak and benign controls, and compares against dedicated safety classifiers. Experiment 2 extends the activation/readout analysis across attack types and models. The claim does not bind the reference's exact number of benchmarks, models, or architecture families, so the proposed broader-but-less-prescriptively-counted evaluation has the required discriminating power.

runs.sufficiency_reasoning: The proposed set directly tests persistence versus elimination, constructs matched successful jailbreak/refusal pairs, localizes and causally manipulates a small head subset, checks persistence in non-suppressed heads, and evaluates a no-training readout against dedicated safety models. It would therefore substantially adjudicate the stated claim. The result would retain important evidential gaps: the causal flip lacks a matched arbitrary-head perturbation control, the contribution of the other heads is observational rather than causal, and the token-level rival explanation is not isolated. These gaps weaken mechanistic specificity but do not prevent the proposed set from testing the claim's main persistence, bypass, sufficiency, persistence-in-other-heads, and detector-quality assertions.
